title: CAN YOU LUST AFTER YOUR OWN SPOUSE? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING YOUR WEDDING VOWS NEVER FIXED.
paragraphs: CAN YOU LUST AFTER YOUR OWN SPOUSE? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING YOUR WEDDING VOWS NEVER FIXED.

You can wear a wedding ring, share a marriage bed, and still misunderstand what God intended intimacy to be. Because marriage makes sexual union honorable, but it does not make selfishness holy. And sometimes the deepest betrayal in a marriage begins long before anyone commits adultery.
There is a question many Christians have never dared to ask out loud.
Not because the Bible is silent about sexuality.
But because the answer might force us to examine something we have spent years defending.
Can you actually lust after the person God has given you permission to love?
Think carefully before answering.
Because somewhere tonight, a wife is lying beside her husband, wondering why she feels more like an obligation than someone cherished.
Somewhere else, a husband is quietly struggling with rejection, wondering whether his desire for his wife makes him selfish.
Somewhere, a Christian couple has stopped talking about intimacy because every conversation ends in guilt, frustration, tears, or silence.
And somewhere, a believer is convinced that because the person they desire is their lawful spouse, everything they want must automatically be righteous.
But what if the real question is not simply whether you desire your spouse?
What if the question is what your desire is doing to the person you promised before God to love?
Because there is a difference between wanting to be close to someone and wanting to consume them.
There is a difference between longing for intimacy and demanding access.
There is a difference between a desire that says, "I want to give myself to you," and an appetite that says, "You exist to satisfy me."
And Scripture makes that difference impossible to ignore.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:28:
"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." (KJV)
Those words should make us tremble—not because sexual attraction is inherently dirty, but because Jesus refuses to separate the outward act from the inward condition of the heart.
In the original Greek, the expression translated "to lust after her" includes the phrase πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn).
The verb epithymeō means to desire, long for, or covet. Depending on the context, that desire may be good or sinful.
That distinction matters enormously.
The Greek word itself does not mean that every experience of sexual attraction is wicked.
In fact, the same family of Greek words appears in Luke 22:15, where Jesus speaks of His earnest desire to eat the Passover with His disciples.
Desire itself is not automatically sin.
What matters is its object, its intention, and whether it submits to God's will.

In Matthew 5, Jesus is confronting a deliberately cultivated desire that violates faithfulness. He is exposing the heart behind adultery, not declaring that a husband sins whenever he is sexually attracted to his wife.
That would contradict the very Scriptures that celebrate marital desire.
And this is where we must be careful.
Matthew 5:28 does not directly teach that desiring your own spouse is adultery. But the rest of Scripture absolutely challenges selfish, degrading, coercive, and unloving behavior within marriage.
A wedding covenant does not turn every attitude into holiness.
A marriage certificate cannot sanctify cruelty.
And a wedding ring is not a license to disregard another person's dignity.
Now consider something beautiful.
Proverbs 5:18–19 tells a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth and to be continually satisfied with her love.
The Hebrew text uses the language of delight and deep affection. The word אַהֲבָה (ahavah) means love, and the passage speaks openly and positively about the joy of marital intimacy.
God is not embarrassed by the desire He designed.
He is not standing in heaven condemning a husband for finding his wife beautiful.
He is not shaming a wife for longing for her husband's affection, touch, or closeness.
Read the Song of Solomon.
There is longing.
There is admiration.
There is romantic pursuit.
There is the unmistakable celebration of physical beauty and marital love.
Song of Solomon 7:10 declares:
"I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me." (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated "desire" is תְּשׁוּקָה (teshuqah), a word associated with strong longing or desire.
Here, that desire appears in the setting of mutual romantic affection.
The beloved does not speak as though being desired is automatically degrading.
She delights in being loved.
This is important because some Christians have been taught to feel guilty for experiencing sexual attraction even within marriage.
They have confused purity with the absence of passion.
They have mistaken holiness for emotional distance.
They have carried shame into a relationship where God intended covenant love, tenderness, faithfulness, and joy.
But God did not create marriage so two people could spend their lives apologizing for finding each other attractive.
Hebrews 13:4 says:
"Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge." (KJV)
The marriage bed is not inherently shameful.
Faithful marital intimacy is not spiritual contamination.
And physical affection does not become sinful simply because it is intense.
But now comes the part that may be uncomfortable.
Just because desire belongs in marriage does not mean every expression of desire honors marriage.
Imagine a husband who approaches his wife with affection only when he wants sex.
He barely listens when she speaks.
He dismisses her exhaustion.
He ignores her emotional pain.
He offers tenderness when he expects something in return, but withdraws it when she says she is not ready.
Eventually, she begins to wonder whether he loves her or merely loves what she can provide.
Or imagine a wife who uses intimacy as a tool to punish, manipulate, humiliate, or control her husband.
His vulnerabilities become weapons.
His longing for affection becomes something she exploits.
Neither situation reflects the self-giving love Scripture commands.
The problem is not that either spouse experiences sexual desire.
The problem is that desire has become detached from love.
And when desire becomes a justification for pressure, manipulation, or disregard, something has gone terribly wrong.
Marriage does not erase personhood.
Your spouse is not a possession.
Your spouse is not a reward for your religious performance.
Your spouse is not a machine designed to meet your needs whenever you press the right buttons.
Your spouse is a human being created in the image of God.
Someone with fears.
Someone with wounds.
Someone with a body that can become tired.
Someone with emotions that can become overwhelmed.
Someone who needs to feel safe, respected, and cherished.
Someone Christ calls you to love—not merely someone you are permitted to desire.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
Read those words again.
Gave himself.
Not demanded everything.
Not exercised selfish control.
Not insisted that his own desires always come first.
Gave himself.
The Greek verb παρέδωκεν (paredōken), translated "gave," comes from paradidōmi, meaning to hand over or give up. In this verse, it describes Christ's self-giving sacrifice.
That is the model Paul places before husbands.
And it is a model that confronts every selfish instinct within us.
Christ did not love His church by exploiting her vulnerability.
He gave Himself for her good.
That does not mean marriage is devoid of sexual pleasure or that spouses must suppress every personal longing.
It means love must govern how those longings are expressed.
The question becomes painfully personal.
When you approach your spouse, do they experience your desire as affection or pressure?
When they are struggling, do you notice?
When they are hurting, do you listen?
When intimacy is difficult, do you seek understanding or immediately assign blame?
Can your spouse be honest with you without fearing punishment, humiliation, or retaliation?
And when your desires are not fulfilled, does your love remain recognizable?
These questions are not designed to shame married people for having sexual needs.
They are designed to expose the difference between mutual intimacy and selfish entitlement.
Because a person can desire their spouse sexually and still fail to love them sacrificially.
That truth should humble every one of us.
Perhaps you are reading this and realizing that you have sometimes approached your marriage more like a consumer than a covenant partner.
Perhaps your spouse has been trying to explain their pain for years, but you interpreted every conversation as rejection.
Perhaps you have been physically present while emotionally absent.
Or perhaps you are the spouse who has carried silent shame because someone convinced you that marriage meant surrendering your right to speak honestly about your own body.
Listen carefully.
God does not require you to call mistreatment holy.
Marriage is a covenant of faithfulness and love, not permission for sexual coercion or abuse.
First Corinthians 7:3–5 speaks about mutual marital responsibilities and warns against unilateral deprivation. But notice something often overlooked: Paul's instruction is reciprocal.
The husband has responsibilities toward the wife.
The wife has responsibilities toward the husband.
And in verse 5, Paul specifically speaks of abstaining for a time by mutual consent.
The Greek expression ἐκ συμφώνου (ek symphōnou) means by agreement or mutual consent.
That phrase matters.
The passage calls spouses toward mutual consideration, not forced compliance.
It must never be used to justify assault, intimidation, or the idea that a spouse loses bodily dignity after marriage.
Biblical mutuality does not erase the obligation to treat one another with patience, kindness, and honor.
And the call to marital faithfulness never authorizes abuse.
Now consider the other side.
What about the husband who deeply desires his wife but feels ashamed because he has heard that lust is always sinful?
What about the wife who feels drawn to her husband, yet worries that passionate attraction makes her spiritually impure?
They need to hear this too.
You do not have to repent for loving the beauty of the person you married.
You do not have to feel ashamed for longing for mutual physical closeness.
You do not have to treat your God-given capacity for attraction as though it were an enemy of holiness.
What you must surrender is the temptation to turn that attraction into selfishness, fantasy that violates faithfulness, pressure, objectification, or control.
There is a world of difference between saying, "You are beautiful, and I long to be close to you," and communicating, "Your feelings do not matter because I want what I want."
One honors the beloved.
The other reduces the beloved to a means of satisfaction.
And sometimes, that difference is revealed not when your spouse says yes, but when your spouse says no.
Can you still be gentle?
Can you still be affectionate?
Can you still be kind?
Can you remain faithful without turning disappointment into punishment?
Can you talk honestly about unmet needs without demanding, threatening, or manipulating?
Because love is not proven only in the moments when you receive what you desire.
Sometimes love becomes clearest in the moments when you choose another person's well-being over immediate gratification.
First Corinthians 13:5 says that love "seeketh not her own."
That does not mean loving spouses can never express their own needs.
It means biblical love is not ruled by selfish insistence.
And here is something else we must not ignore.
A marriage can suffer from sexual distance without either spouse being the villain.
Illness can change intimacy.
Trauma can affect trust.
Childbirth, exhaustion, grief, medication, disability, depression, unresolved conflict, and other burdens can make physical closeness complicated.
Sometimes couples need patient conversation.
Sometimes they need medical care.
Sometimes they need wise pastoral guidance or qualified marriage counseling.
Sometimes they need to rebuild emotional safety before physical intimacy can become joyful again.
And sometimes a person needs protection from abuse rather than another sermon telling them to try harder.
Not every painful marriage problem can be solved by quoting a verse and demanding immediate change.
God's Word calls us to truth.
And truth requires us to see people as they really are, including the wounds they carry.
But there is another wound this conversation must address.
Pornography.
Because some husbands and wives have unknowingly brought the expectations of pornography into their marriages.
They compare real human bodies to carefully manufactured images.
They expect constant availability.
They mistake performance for intimacy.
They grow dissatisfied with the very person they once prayed to marry.
And slowly, the spouse who was supposed to be cherished begins to feel inadequate.
This is one way sinful lust can corrupt marital intimacy.
Not because the spouse is the wrong person to desire.
But because desire has been trained to consume rather than cherish.
Pornography can cultivate habits of objectification, secrecy, comparison, and discontent that undermine marital trust.
And the solution is not to blame the spouse for failing to compete with fantasy.
The solution begins with truth, repentance, accountability, and renewed faithfulness.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:29–30 that we must deal radically with what leads us into sin.
His graphic language is a serious call to remove occasions of sin, not an instruction to physically injure ourselves.
For someone trapped in pornography, that may mean removing access, seeking accountability, confessing deception, and pursuing competent support.
For someone whose desire has become controlling, it may mean admitting that entitlement has been masquerading as love.
For someone whose marriage has become emotionally cold, it may mean finally listening instead of defending.
For someone who has been mistreated, it may mean seeking safety, trusted support, and appropriate professional help.
Repentance does not look identical in every marriage.
But it always requires honesty before God.
And perhaps this is where the Holy Spirit is speaking to someone reading these words.
You have defended your behavior by saying, "But we are married."
You have assumed that being legally entitled to a relationship means every demand within that relationship is righteous.
You have confused covenant privilege with personal ownership.
And now you are beginning to understand something.
The person you married is not merely someone you have the right to touch. They are someone you have the responsibility to love.
That truth changes everything.
It changes how you speak.
How you listen.
How you respond to vulnerability.
How you handle rejection.
How you pursue reconciliation.
How you confess sin.
How you treat the person who sees you when no one else does.
Because Christian marriage is not ultimately about proving that your desires are legitimate.
It is about learning to bring those desires under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that is where the Gospel enters this conversation with extraordinary power.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our behavior.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to forgive what we cannot undo and transform what we cannot repair by our own strength.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we perfected our marriages.
Not after we conquered every selfish impulse.
Not after we became worthy of grace.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
And that matters because some people reading this article are carrying regret.
You remember the night you spoke cruelly.
The time you ignored your spouse's tears.
The seasons when you treated intimacy like a transaction.
The secrecy you allowed to grow.
The bitterness you refused to confront.
The love you withheld.
The trust you broke.
And you wonder whether God can still restore someone like you.
The answer begins at the cross.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ for those who repent and trust in Him.
There is grace for the person who finally stops making excuses.
There is mercy for the believer who confesses sin rather than concealing it.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
But grace is not permission to keep harming someone.
Repentance is more than feeling guilty after reading a powerful article.
It bears fruit.
It tells the truth.
It accepts responsibility.
It stops blaming others.
It seeks help where needed.
It respects boundaries.
It makes restitution where possible.
It understands that broken trust may take time to rebuild.
And it does not demand immediate forgiveness, reconciliation, or renewed intimacy as proof that the injured person has obeyed God.
True repentance refuses to use the language of grace as another instrument of control.
That is how we know the Gospel is doing more than stirring emotion.
It is changing the direction of a life.
And maybe tonight, that transformation begins with one difficult sentence.
"I'm sorry. I have been thinking about what I want more than how you feel."
Or perhaps:
"I have been so afraid of being rejected that I stopped hearing your pain."
Or:
"I have confused physical closeness with emotional safety, and I want to learn how to love you better."
Or even:
"I need help, because what has been happening in our marriage is not healthy."
Those words may not solve everything overnight.
But honest confession can become the beginning of a different story.
A story where tenderness returns.
Where trust is rebuilt patiently.
Where forgiveness is sought without being demanded.
Where desire becomes an expression of love instead of a substitute for it.
Where two imperfect people learn that the marriage covenant was never meant to replace daily obedience to Christ.
And where, if a relationship is unsafe, the wounded person is supported in seeking protection rather than pressured into remaining in danger.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely expose our sin.
He offers forgiveness and calls us into a new way of living.
Ephesians 4:22–24 speaks of putting off the old self, being renewed in the spirit of our minds, and putting on the new self created after God in righteousness and true holiness.
That transformation reaches even the most private places of our lives.
Even our marriages.
Even our desires.
Even the thoughts we have never confessed aloud.
So can you lust after your own spouse?
Here is the answer we must carry carefully.
Sexually desiring your spouse is not inherently sinful. Scripture celebrates faithful marital attraction, delight, and mutual intimacy.

But a person can express sexual desire within marriage in sinful ways—through selfishness, coercion, degrading treatment, objectification, manipulation, or a refusal to love the spouse as a whole person.
The biblical question is not whether passion exists.
It is whether passion is governed by covenant love, faithfulness, holiness, and the dignity of the person being loved.
Your spouse is not your enemy.
Desire is not automatically your enemy.
But sin is never your friend, even when it hides behind something God created good.
And the answer is not less Jesus in your marriage.
It is more surrender to Him.
More truth.
More compassion.
More humility.
More repentance.
More grace.
More love that actually looks like Christ.
If your spouse could describe how your desire makes them feel, what would they say?
Cherished?
Safe?
Beautiful?
Respected?
Or pressured, unseen, and alone?
And if you are the one who has been wounded, what would it look like to begin believing that your dignity matters to God too?
You do not have to answer publicly with details that belong in a safe and private conversation.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
Pray.
Listen.
Confess.
Seek help.
Forgive where forgiveness is possible.
Establish boundaries where boundaries are necessary.
And ask the Lord to teach you how to love without using another person.

If God has brought you through a season of brokenness and restoration, your testimony may encourage someone who has nearly given up. Share what you are comfortable sharing, without exposing your spouse's private struggles.
Not to publicly accuse your spouse.
Not to embarrass someone.
But because a biblical conversation about marriage may reach a person who has never heard these truths explained with both conviction and compassion.
Because what we are building is not simply another page filled with religious content.
Our prayer is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and find the courage to surrender what needs to change.
Scripture teaches the importance of cheerful, willing giving. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver.
And that is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not from fear.
Not from guilt.
Not because God's favor can be purchased.
But if you believe in this mission and have the means to help, your partnership can make a genuine difference in sustaining and expanding the work.
We want the Word of God to reach people.
We want believers to be equipped.
We want marriages to be strengthened by truth rather than religious confusion.
We want the broken to hear about the Savior who forgives sinners and transforms lives.
We want those who are spiritually hungry to have resources that help them grow.
And we want every article, every book, every testimony, and every act of generosity to point beyond Gospel Warrior to Jesus Christ Himself.
A sincere comment may remind another believer that they are not alone in their struggle.
And that matters.
Because this article was never merely about sex.
It was about the human heart.
It was about the difference between possessing and cherishing.
Between taking and giving.
Between religious excuses and genuine repentance.
Between shame that drives people into hiding and grace that calls sinners into the light.
It was about a Savior who does not merely tell us what love should look like.
He showed us.
At the cross.
Where the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Where mercy met our guilt.
Where forgiveness was purchased by His blood.
Where the greatest expression of love was not selfish consumption, but sacrificial giving.
So tonight, when you look at the person you married, remember this.
They are not simply the answer to your longing.
They are a neighbor you are commanded to love.
A person whose dignity matters to God.
A soul whose well-being must never be sacrificed on the altar of your appetite.

And if your marriage has been damaged by sin, remember that Christ can change hearts, empower repentance, and guide people toward what is true and good. Restoration may require time, accountability, professional help, and, where necessary, safety and separation from harm. But no failure is beyond the reach of God's power to forgive the repentant sinner.
May your marriage never become a place where Scripture is used to justify selfishness.
May your desire never become louder than your compassion.
May your wedding vows be reflected not only in the promises you made before an altar, but in the way you treat one another when nobody else is watching.
And may Jesus Christ be glorified in the love you give, the truth you speak, the sins you confess, and the grace you learn to extend.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that your spouse might stop desiring you. It is that they might spend years being desired without ever feeling truly loved.
